doc.title: Mose Allison — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: Leaving Atlantic in 1980 and Bruce Lundvall at Elektra-Musician
summary: He left over an advance dispute and signed with Lundvall, who never told him what to do.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Record labels, producers and the business of making albums

blocks.x: You left Atlantic Records in 1980. There was a certain acrimony at the end. You wanted to be paid an advance commensurate with some of their other artists, and they didn’t want to give you that advance, and you felt you weren’t being promoted enough by then, and they felt you weren’t compromising enough to do things that were commercial, and so on. They gave you the option that you should either accept your usual advance or be released from the contract, and you did. Then you signed with the Elektra-Musician label, which Bruce Lundvall had just taken over.
Do you remember anything about Bruce Lundvall approaching you, or...
No. I liked Bruce Lundvall, and... He was a fan of mine way before...when I made “Baby, Please Don’t Go” on Columbia. He became a fan with that, and he’d listened to that several times.
How did you meet up with him? Did he approach you, Dad?
No. I don’t know how I met him. I used... The guy we knew in Boulder, Colorado... Well, it wasn’t Boulder.
Colorado Springs. Well, I don’t remember how it started. I just remember that you’ve always really liked Bruce Lundvall, and he didn’t ever tell you what to do.
Seems very important to keeping a good relationship with you.
....(?—16:08).... you’d just call him up? Yeah, he was calling and saying, ‘I want to make it when you’re ready...”
